title: CFA Ethics 38: Applying it in the Vietnamese market - where the Code is stricter than the law
subtitle: Personal relationships, boardroom information, and the areas domestic rules have not yet reached
whyItMatters: Standard I(A) says follow whichever is stricter, the law or the Code. For a practitioner in Vietnam the common direction is the Code being stricter - and that is the direction nobody enforces but you.
openingQuestion: A personal contact tells you company X is about to announce an exceptional set of results. That person does not work at X but heard it from a friend who does. May you trade?
openingOptions: Yes, because it reached you through several layers and is no longer inside information
No: the information is still material and not yet public
Yes, provided you paid nothing to obtain it
Yes, provided you disclose the source in your research note
explanation: The number of intermediaries does not launder the information. Two conditions remain: it is material, and it is not yet broadly public. The third condition - that it originated with someone breaching a duty of confidentiality - also remains, and not knowing exactly who was first does not remove it where the circumstances show the information could only have come from inside. In a market where personal relationships play a large part in the flow of information, this arises far more often than the classic insider dealing scenario - and it is harder to recognise, because it arrives in an ordinary conversation.

summary.keyIdea: In a market with dense personal relationships and gaps in the law, the Code is not a supplementary layer but the binding constraint actually applying to you.
summary.commonMistake: Relying on domestic law not covering it. The Code is the personal undertaking of whoever carries the designation, and it applies whichever standard is stricter.

application.title: The particular situation
application.message: Dense personal relationships blur the information boundary. The question does not change: has this information been released to every investor yet.

sections.text: The CFA standards are written for a global market. Applying them in an emerging market exposes exactly the places where the Code is stricter than the law - and those are the places nobody enforces but you.

News of unpublished results reaches you through three acquaintances. The number of intermediaries does not launder it: two conditions remain - material, and not yet broadly public. The third, that it originated with someone breaching a duty of confidentiality, also remains; not knowing exactly who was first does not remove it where the circumstances show the information could only have come from inside.

sections.label: Why this form is harder to recognise
sections.text: It does not arrive as a secret meeting but as an ordinary conversation. In a market where personal relationships play a large part in the flow of information, this arises far more often than classic insider dealing.
Three places where the Code runs ahead of the law

items: VI(A) on disclosing conflicts is broader than a declaration rule tied to an ownership threshold - below the legal threshold, disclosure may still be required by the Code.
III(C) requires suitability to be assessed at the portfolio level, while the rules usually stop at classifying an investor as professional or not.
GIPS is voluntary, so the gap between the legal minimum disclosure and what GIPS requires is exactly the territory of professional ethics.

lines: Where the law is still developing, professional standards do not become lighter.
They are the only part left.

diagram.label: Material + not yet public = do not trade
The number of intermediaries does not launder the information
Looser domestic law does not release the duty under the Code
The "Code is stricter" direction has no enforcer but you

realWorldExample.company: Three areas where the Code usually runs ahead of domestic rules
realWorldExample.description: First, disclosing conflicts of interest: many rules only require declaring ownership above a threshold, while Standard VI(A) requires disclosing anything that could reasonably be expected to affect judgment. Second, suitability: the rules usually stop at classifying investors, while Standard III(C) requires assessment at the portfolio level for each individual. Third, performance presentation: GIPS is voluntary everywhere, so the entire gap between it and the regulatory minimum is territory bound only by professional ethics.

quiz.question: What about material information that has passed through several intermediaries?
options: Usable if you do not know who the original source was
It becomes public information after passing three or more people
Still material and still not public, so it cannot be traded on
Usable provided you paid nothing to obtain the information
quiz.explanation: The two conditions - material and not yet public - do not depend on the route the information took.

quiz.question: Why is the "Code is stricter than the law" direction so often overlooked?
options: Because CFA Institute does not handle violations occurring abroad
Because the Code of Ethics has no force outside the United States
Because domestic law always takes precedence in application
Because no authority enforces it except the practitioner themselves
quiz.explanation: No external sanction means compliance rests entirely on that person's own decision.

quiz.question: Where does Standard VI(A) go beyond an ordinary ownership declaration rule?
options: It requires disclosing anything that could affect judgment
It requires declaring to the regulator instead of to clients
It requires disclosing the analyst's entire personal portfolio
It requires quarterly disclosure rather than disclosure on arising
quiz.explanation: An ownership threshold is a number; Standard VI(A)'s test is effect on judgment, and it covers far more ground.

quiz.question: Why is information arriving through personal relationships harder to recognise?
options: Because information through personal relationships is usually inaccurate
Because it arrives in an ordinary conversation, with no signal
Because current law has no definition for this form of information
Because the listener has no way of verifying the information
quiz.explanation: Classic insider dealing has an obvious setting; a story over dinner does not - and that is what makes it more common.

quiz.question: Does GIPS have binding legal force in Vietnam?
options: Yes, for fund management companies with foreign ownership
Yes, it has been written into domestic regulation as mandatory
No, GIPS is voluntary in every market including Vietnam
No, and it has no relevance to the domestic market at all
quiz.explanation: Voluntary does not mean unimportant - large institutional investors treat it as a screening condition, and once claimed it must be complied with fully.

keyTakeaways: The number of intermediaries does not launder material non-public information
The "Code is stricter than the law" direction has no enforcer but you
VI(A) is broader than a declaration rule tied to an ownership threshold
III(C) requires suitability at portfolio level, not merely investor classification
GIPS is voluntary, so the gap to the legal minimum is the territory of ethics

practicePrompt.question: Over a meal you hear that a listed company is about to make a major change to its leadership. The speaker is a friend of a board member. What should you do?
options: Trade as normal, since you are not an insider at the company
Do not trade that security, and report it to compliance
Verify the information first, and then decide whether to trade
Share it with colleagues so you can assess its reliability together
practicePrompt.explanation: Verifying sounds reasonable and runs the wrong way: verifying correctly only makes you more certain you hold material non-public information. Passing it on is a separate violation. The only safe handling is not to trade and to take it into the compliance channel - which has tools you personally do not.
